numberItems.stem: How many situations does the handbook list where you MUST evacuate a school bus?
numberItems.explanation: There are 5 mandatory evacuations: fire or threat of fire, stalled on or next to a railroad crossing, position may change, imminent crash, and HazMat spill. 11 is the number of general evacuation steps (p. 10-7).

numberItems.stem: In a roadside evacuation, where is the safe place for the students?
options: At least 100 ft off the road, toward oncoming traffic
At least 300 ft off the road, toward oncoming traffic
At least 100 ft off the road, away from oncoming traffic
numberItems.explanation: Take students at least 100 ft off the road in the direction of oncoming traffic, so debris does not hit them if a car strikes the bus. 300 ft is the HazMat distance (p. 10-7).

numberItems.stem: Hazardous materials have spilled near the bus. Where should the students go?
options: Downwind, at least 300 ft from the bus
Upwind, at least 100 ft from the bus
Upwind, at least 300 ft from the bus
numberItems.explanation: For spilled HazMat, go upwind, at least 300 ft from the bus, so fumes blow away from the students (p. 10-7).

numberItems.stem: You have no working radio or phone and no passing driver or resident can call for help. As a last resort, how many older, responsible students may you send for help?
numberItems.explanation: As a last resort, send 2 older, responsible students for help (p. 10-8).

numberItems.stem: About how far before a railroad crossing should a school bus driver turn on the hazard lights?
numberItems.explanation: Turn on the hazard lights about 200 ft before the crossing so others know what you will do (p. 10-10).

numberItems.stem: At a railroad crossing, what is the FARTHEST a school bus should stop from the nearest rail?
numberItems.explanation: Stop no closer than 15 ft and no farther than 50 ft from the nearest rail, where you can see the tracks best (p. 10-10).

numberItems.stem: What is the rule of thumb for the containment (storage) space you need past the tracks?
numberItems.explanation: "If it will not fit, do not commit": you need the bus length plus 15 ft clear of the tracks (p. 10-10).

numberItems.stem: ABS is required on air-brake vehicles built on or after what date?
options: Any date; every air-brake bus must have it
numberItems.explanation: Air-brake vehicles built on or after March 1, 1998 must have ABS; March 1, 1999 is the hydraulic-brake date (p. 10-11).

numberItems.stem: Hydraulic-brake trucks and buses built on or after March 1, 1999 must have ABS if their GVWR is at least:
numberItems.explanation: Hydraulic-brake trucks and buses with a GVWR of 10,000 lb or more built on or after March 1, 1999 must have ABS (p. 10-11).

numberItems.stem: On older ABS systems, how long may the yellow malfunction lamp stay on after start-up?
options: Until you are going over 5 mph
numberItems.explanation: On older systems the lamp may stay on until you are going over 5 mph; on newer buses it goes out quickly after the bulb check (p. 10-12).

numberItems.stem: The ABS lamp comes on while you are driving. What may have happened?
options: ABS may be lost at 1 or more wheels
numberItems.explanation: If the lamp stays on after the bulb check or comes on while driving, you may have lost ABS at 1 or more wheels; you still have normal brakes (p. 10-12).

numberItems.stem: [CA] In which situation may you use the roof-mounted white strobe light?
options: Driving at night in clear weather
Fog that cuts visibility to 500 ft or less
Light rain with visibility well over 500 ft
numberItems.explanation: [CA] Use the strobe only when visibility is 500 ft or less because of fog, rain, snow, smoke, dust or similar conditions (CVC §25257.7) (p. 10-12).
